title: Path to Happiness Revealed in New Book

image.attribution: U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Chad Runge / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain.

main_content:
Everyone wants to be happy, but true happiness eludes many of us. Raj Raghunathan thinks he knows why.

The marketing professor at the University of Texas in Austin is known as Dr. Happy-smarts. He’s been teaching a very popular course on happiness for seven years, attracting thousands of students, both at the University of Texas and at the Indian School of Business in Hyderabad, as well as online.

[Things] get in the way of being happy, and in his book, “If You’re So Smart, Why Aren’t You Happy?”, Raghunathan calls them “happiness sins.” They include chasing superiority, wanting to be the center of attention, the desire to control others and outcomes, and not giving happiness much priority. He says the smarter and more successful you are, the greater the chance that you commit these sins.

To steer our mindset toward the abundance approach and undo all the “happiness sins,” the professor recommends several exercises:

Prioritize happiness.  Remind yourself, especially before making important decisions, that happiness is your goal in life. Express gratitude to somebody who has a positive influence in your life. Practice creative altruism, random acts of kindness. We really derive a lot of joy from doing good for other people. Lead a healthy lifestyle.  Sleep well, eat well, exercise. Learn to forgive.  It turns out that when we hold grudges, it actually hurts us more than it hurts the person against whom we have this grudge. Bring yourself to believe that what’s happening, even if it’s negative, is eventually going to be a good thing for you. Practice mindfulness, just being in the moment.

Practicing those exercises, Raghunathan says, can help you respond to the question posed in the title of his book with the answer, “I’m happier now.”
